levels.green: The farmer can handle it alone. Give simple advice, no expert needed.
levels.yellow: Needs tools, parts, or skill the farmer may not have. Offer an expert service or a human callback.
levels.red: Fire or safety danger. Call 112 first, then arrange urgent follow-up.

meta.note: Starter content for the agent knowledge base. LahiTapiola experts should confirm the details before real use.

hazards.name: Hay and straw self-heating
hazards.check_question: Have you checked the temperature of your stored hay and straw?

green.situation: Hay is stored dry, but the temperature has not been checked recently.
green.short_summary: Probe the stack temperature, keep hay dry, and keep stacks away from barn walls.
detailed_info: Use a hay probe or long thermometer and take readings at several spots deep inside the stack, not just near the surface.
Write the readings down with the date so you can spot a steady rise over time.
Check more often in the first weeks after storage and after any rain or damp weather.
Keep stacks dry and leave an air gap between the stack and the barn walls.
Avoid storing hay that was baled damp. If you have to, keep it separate and watch it closely.

yellow.situation: Hay was stored damp, is stacked against a barn wall, or there are no readings at all and the stack cannot easily be moved.
yellow.difficult_for_farmer: Judging how risky a damp or tightly packed stack is, and handling it safely without making it worse.
yellow.short_summary: Monitor closely, do not pull the stack apart, and ask a LahiTapiola expert for advice.
detailed_info: Take temperature readings every day and keep a written log of them.
Do not pull the stack apart or open it up. The extra air can make a hot stack ignite.
Move machinery, fuel, and other valuables away from the stack and the wall behind it.
Keep extinguishers and a water source close, and make sure everyone on the farm knows about the stack.
Share your readings with a LahiTapiola expert so they can advise on the safest next step.

red.situation: The stack feels hot, smells burnt or sweet and smoky, shows smoke or steam, or the temperature keeps rising.
red.difficult_for_farmer: Everything. Opening the stack or fighting it alone is dangerous.
red.short_summary: Call 112 now, do not open up the stack, and keep people and animals away.
detailed_info: Call 112 immediately and give the farm address.
Do not pull the stack apart or dig into it. Fresh air can turn smouldering hay into open flames.
Keep people and animals well away from the stack and the nearest buildings.
If it is safe, move machinery and fuel away from the area.
Meet the fire service at the gate and tell them where the stack is and what you have seen.

hazards.name: Barn wiring and dust
hazards.check_question: Have you cleaned the dust off the lights, wiring and motors in your barn?

green.situation: Lights, motors, and fittings are dusty, but the wiring looks fine and nothing has tripped or heated up.
green.difficult_for_farmer: Nothing difficult at this level, as long as you only clean and never open electrical panels.
green.short_summary: Switch off the power, then clean dust and cobwebs off lights, wiring, and motors.
detailed_info: Switch off the power to the area first and let motors and lamps cool down.
Use a dry brush or a vacuum. Never use water on electrical parts.
Clean light fittings, motor housings, fans, and the outside of cables and sockets.
Do not open fuse boxes or panels. Only clean the outside.
Keep walkways clear and do not store hay, straw, or cardboard against electrical equipment.
Repeat the cleaning every season, and more often in dusty periods.

yellow.situation: Fuses trip often, lights flicker, plugs or cables feel warm, the wiring is old, or it has not been inspected in many years.
yellow.difficult_for_farmer: Finding the real fault and fixing wiring safely. Repairs should only be done by a qualified electrician.
yellow.short_summary: Stop using the affected circuit if you can, and book an electrician for an inspection.
detailed_info: Write down which circuit or area has the problem and what you notice, such as tripping, flickering, or warm plugs.
Do not keep resetting a breaker that trips again and again. It is trying to protect you.
Do not use extension cords as permanent wiring, and do not overload sockets.
Do not try to repair wiring yourself.
Book an electrician for a full inspection and share your notes with them.

red.situation: There is a burning smell from electrical equipment, scorch marks, sparks, a very hot socket, or smoke.
red.difficult_for_farmer: Everything. Electrical fires can spread quickly and are not safe to fight alone.
red.short_summary: Cut the main power only if it is safe, get out, and call 112 if there is smoke or fire.
detailed_info: If there is smoke or fire, leave first and call 112 immediately.
Switch off the main power only if you can reach it safely and it is dry.
Never throw water on an electrical fire.
Get people and animals out if it is safe to do so.
Do not turn the power back on until an electrician has inspected the installation.

hazards.name: Grain dryer
hazards.check_question: Has the grain dryer been cleaned and checked before this season?

green.situation: The dryer runs normally but has not been cleaned yet this season.
green.short_summary: Clear out chaff and dust before the season, and never leave it running unattended.
detailed_info: Switch the dryer off, disconnect the power and the fuel supply, and let it cool fully before cleaning.
Remove chaff and dust from the burner area, fans, ducts, and floors.
Check for built up debris, and for nests or stored items near the burner.
Do a short test run with someone present and watch for anything unusual.
Stay nearby whenever it runs, and keep an extinguisher within reach.

yellow.situation: The burner is hard to light, the flame looks uneven, safety cutouts or controls act oddly, or there has been no technician check for a long time.
yellow.difficult_for_farmer: Diagnosing burner and control faults, and testing safety cutouts. This needs a trained technician.
yellow.short_summary: Do not run it until a technician has checked it.
detailed_info: Stop using the dryer and write down what you noticed.
Never bypass or disable safety controls to keep it running.
Do not adjust the burner yourself.
Book a dryer service and ask the technician to check the safety cutouts and controls too.
Book early. Technicians get busy right before harvest.

red.situation: There is fire or smoke in the dryer, a strong smell of fuel or gas, or it keeps overheating.
red.difficult_for_farmer: Everything. A dryer fire can spread fast to grain and buildings.
red.short_summary: Shut it down only if safe, leave the area, and call 112.
detailed_info: Call 112 immediately.
Use the emergency stop or cut the fuel supply only if you can reach it safely.
Do not try to fight a growing fire or stay near a fuel smell.
Keep people and animals away from the dryer and nearby buildings.
Do not use the dryer again until a technician has inspected it.

hazards.name: Fire extinguishers and smoke alarms
hazards.check_question: Are your fire extinguishers in date, and are they near the exits?

green.situation: Extinguishers exist, but the farmer is not sure about the date, the gauge, or where they are placed.
green.short_summary: Check the date and gauge, put extinguishers near the exits, and test the smoke alarms.
detailed_info: Look at the service label for the date of the last check.
Check that the pressure gauge is in the marked safe zone and that the pin and seal are intact.
Look for dents, rust, or damage on the body and hose.
Mount extinguishers near exits at a height you can reach easily, and tell everyone on the farm where they are.
Test the smoke alarms and replace the batteries if needed.

yellow.situation: An extinguisher is overdue for service, the gauge is outside the safe zone, it is damaged, or some buildings have none.
yellow.difficult_for_farmer: Servicing or refilling extinguishers, and choosing the right type and number for each building.
yellow.short_summary: Do not rely on faulty extinguishers. Book a service or replacement.
detailed_info: Write down which extinguishers are overdue or damaged and where they are.
Keep other precautions in place until they are serviced, such as clearing dust and removing fuel from barns.
Book an extinguisher service or replacement.
Ask the provider which types suit the barn, fuel store, and machinery sheds, and how many you need.
Ask them to show where each one should be mounted.

red.situation: A fire has started and there is no working extinguisher, or the fire is already growing.
red.difficult_for_farmer: Fighting a growing fire. Personal safety comes first.
red.short_summary: Leave and call 112. Do not fight a growing fire.
detailed_info: Call 112 immediately.
Only try a very small fire if you have a working extinguisher and a clear exit behind you.
If the fire is growing, get people and animals out if it is safe, and stay away.
Meet the fire service at the gate and tell them what is burning and where.
Replace or service all extinguishers afterwards.

hazards.name: Tractor and harvester servicing
hazards.check_question: Have your tractor and harvester been serviced before this season?

green.situation: The machines run fine, but the pre-season service has not been done yet.
green.short_summary: Check oil, filters, belts, tires, and lights before the season.
detailed_info: Check engine oil, hydraulic fluid, and coolant levels.
Inspect the air filter, belts, and hoses for wear or cracks.
Check tire condition and pressure, and test all lights.
Grease the moving parts and clean the radiator and engine area of crop residue.
Keep a simple service log and stock spare filters and belts.

yellow.situation: Service intervals were missed, or there are leaks, strange noises, warning lights, or hard starting.
yellow.difficult_for_farmer: Finding the cause of noises, leaks, and warning lights, and repairing hydraulics, engines, or brakes.
yellow.short_summary: Avoid heavy use and book a mechanic before harvest.
detailed_info: Write down the symptoms, such as when the noise happens or where the leak is.
Do not ignore warning lights or keep working a machine that is getting worse.
Avoid long or heavy use until it has been checked.
Book a mechanic early, since workshops fill up around harvest.
Ask them to check brakes, steering, and anything involving fuel or hydraulic lines.

red.situation: There is a fuel or hydraulic leak near hot parts, smoke, a burning smell, or brake or steering failure.
red.difficult_for_farmer: Everything. A leak near hot parts can start a fire, and failed brakes or steering are not safe to work with.
red.short_summary: Stop the engine if safe, get away from the machine, and call 112 if there is fire or smoke.
detailed_info: Stop the machine and switch off the engine only if it is safe to do so.
Get away from the machine and keep others away.
If there is smoke or fire, call 112 immediately.
Do not restart the machine or drive it to the workshop.
Have it towed or repaired on site by a mechanic.

hazards.name: Theft of machines, tools, and diesel
hazards.check_question: Are your machines, tools and diesel locked up overnight?

green.situation: Things are usually locked up, but there is no lighting, no photos, and no record of serial numbers.
green.short_summary: Lock everything up at night, add lighting, and record serial numbers.
detailed_info: Lock sheds and fuel stores, and lock the machines and fuel caps.
Never leave keys in vehicles or in obvious spots near them.
Add outdoor lighting near the yard and sheds.
Photograph serial numbers and keep a copy somewhere off the farm, such as in the cloud or with family.
Tell trusted neighbors when you are away.

yellow.situation: Valuable equipment is left in an open yard, a past theft or attempt has happened, or there have been incidents nearby.
yellow.difficult_for_farmer: Choosing and installing cameras, alarms, trackers, and secure storage.
yellow.short_summary: Improve physical security with help from a security installer.
detailed_info: Move the most valuable equipment into a locked building if you can.
Ask a security installer about lighting, cameras, alarms, and GPS trackers for machines.
Consider anchoring heavy tools or equipment so they are harder to move.
Report any suspicious activity to the police.
Ask for a LahiTapiola callback if you want to discuss how to protect your equipment.

red.situation: A theft is happening right now, or intruders are on the farm.
red.short_summary: Stay safe, do not confront anyone, and call 112.
detailed_info: Stay inside and call 112 immediately.
Do not confront the people. Equipment can be replaced, you cannot.
Note what you see, such as vehicles, number of people, and direction they went.
Do not touch the area afterwards until the police say it is fine.
Ask for a LahiTapiola callback to discuss next steps.

hazards.name: Working alone in risky places
hazards.check_question: When you work alone with machinery or in manure pits, does someone know where you are?

green.situation: The farmer sometimes works alone and carries a phone, but nobody knows the plan for the day.
green.short_summary: Agree a check-in time with someone, and always carry a charged phone.
detailed_info: Pick one person, such as family or a neighbor, and agree a time to check in each day.
Tell them roughly where you will be working.
Keep your phone charged and on you, not in the cab or in the house.
Agree what they should do if you do not check in, for example call you, then come and look.
Put emergency numbers and the farm address near the phone.

yellow.situation: The farmer regularly works alone in manure pits, tanks, or other confined spaces, or with heavy machinery, without training or gas detection.
yellow.difficult_for_farmer: Confined space and pit work needs gas detection equipment and proper training. Gas can be deadly without any warning smell.
yellow.short_summary: Never enter pits or confined spaces alone. Get gas detection and safety training.
detailed_info: Do not enter a manure pit, tank, or other confined space alone, even briefly.
Ventilate before any work, and keep the opening clear.
Use a proper gas detector and make sure someone stays outside as an observer.
Look into safety training for confined space work.
Ask for a LahiTapiola callback if you want help finding training or equipment.

red.situation: Someone is down, injured, or not responding, or there is a gas smell in a pit or enclosed space.
red.difficult_for_farmer: Everything. Going in after the person is how many people get hurt.
red.short_summary: Do not go in. Call 112 immediately.
detailed_info: Call 112 right away and give the farm address.
Do not enter the pit or space to rescue the person. Gas can overcome you in seconds.
If you can do it safely from outside, ventilate the space.
Send someone to the gate to guide the responders in.
Stay on the phone and follow the instructions you are given.

hazards.name: Who runs the farm if the farmer is sick or injured
hazards.check_question: If you were out sick or injured for two weeks, does someone know the daily routine on the farm?

green.situation: Someone informally knows the routine, but nothing is written down.
green.short_summary: Write a one page sheet with routines and contacts, and share it with your backup person.
detailed_info: List the daily tasks, such as feeding, milking, and machine checks, with times and quantities.
Add key contacts, such as the vet, mechanic, supplier, and neighbors.
Note where keys, codes, and important documents are kept.
Give a copy to your backup person and keep one in the house.
Review the sheet at the start of each season.

yellow.situation: Nobody could run the farm if the farmer were ill or injured for a couple of weeks.
yellow.difficult_for_farmer: Finding someone reliable and trained to cover the work, which may take time or outside help.
yellow.short_summary: Find and brief a backup person, and ask for a LahiTapiola callback about your options.
detailed_info: Think about relatives, neighbors, or other farmers who could step in, and ask them.
Walk the person through the daily routine and the equipment while you are healthy.
Look into local farm relief or substitute services.
Write the one page routine sheet and share it.
Ask for a LahiTapiola callback to talk through how to plan for this.

red.situation: The farmer is ill or injured right now, animals or machines need urgent care, and nobody can cover.
red.short_summary: Call 112 if it is serious, then call your backup contact and ask for an urgent callback.
detailed_info: If it is a medical emergency, call 112 first.
Then call family, a neighbor, or your backup person and ask them to cover the urgent tasks.
Give them the one page routine sheet if you have one, or tell them the most urgent tasks first, such as feeding and milking.
Ask for an urgent LahiTapiola callback so someone can help arrange cover.
Focus on getting better. Animals and machines can wait a short while for the right help.
